case.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit
case.limits: It drew one of the most cited dissents in intellectual property, warning that overprotecting identity taxes the public domain, and later courts have policed its edges. It is powerful in advertising contexts and contested everywhere else.
case.holding: A robot dressed and posed to evoke Vanna White in an advertisement could violate her right of publicity, because the right protects identity however it is evoked, not just name, likeness or voice.
case.case_name: White v. Samsung Electronics America, Inc.
case.why_ai_cites_it: The case that stretched publicity rights to cover evocation by machine. Plaintiffs cite it for the claim that an AI rendering need not copy a face or voice to appropriate a person, resembling them in the ways that identify them is enough, which is the outer theory in digital-replica and deepfake suits.

reading.body:
*White v. Samsung* is the primary authority for the argument that an AI output violates a person's right of publicity without copying their face, voice, or name, because the Ninth Circuit held in 1992 that evoking identity by any means is enough.

The holding turned on a robot styled to suggest Vanna White in a Samsung advertisement. The court reasoned that the right of publicity protects the identity itself, not merely its most literal expressions. That logic transfers directly to AI contexts: a generated image, a synthetic voice, or a behavioral imitation could appropriate a person without reproducing any single protected element. Plaintiffs in digital-replica and deepfake litigation cite the case for precisely that outer theory, where resemblance rather than copying is the operative act.

The case carries documented limits. It produced one of the most cited dissents in intellectual property, which warned that extending publicity rights this far burdens the public domain. Later courts have pulled back at its edges, and the holding is described as powerful in advertising contexts and contested elsewhere. The data does not say which later courts imposed those limits, how they bounded the doctrine, or how any specific AI defendant has fared when the theory has been tested.
